web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Multiples, Reverse DCF and Peers
book_title: Why the Price Is What It Is
question: What growth is the market still pricing in at ₹171.59, and why does the valuation fail once spent cash and governance risk are priced honestly?

epigraph.quote: Either we may raise funds through a QIP preferential or we may raise debentures or we may go down debt. It is not decided yet.
epigraph.author: Shazad Rustomji, Chairman, CEO and Managing Director, Q2 and H1 FY27 earnings call, 19 November 2026 [36]

web_blocks.html: Start with two clearly dated market prices so every ratio stays exact. On the 23 November 2026 NSE market-facts ledger, Stallion closed at ₹180.48 per share. That implied a ₹2,095 crore market capitalisation on 11.61 crore shares [14][32]. Two sessions later, on the 25 November live TradingView close, the stock dropped 4.93% to ₹171.59 [32]. Screener-basis market capitalisation fell to ₹1,992 crore, while TradingView shows ₹2,104 crore on its share count [14][32]. Even after a 38.5% drop from its ₹279 high, the stock stays expensive against weaker cash flow, late plants, and integrated peers.

web_blocks.title: The multiples, the shrinking cash cushion, and vendor differences

web_blocks.html: We compute every valuation multiple at the 25 November live TradingView close of ₹171.59, alongside the 23 November NSE ledger close of ₹180.48. We use September 2026 balance-sheet net cash rather than stale March 2026 cash [1][14][36][38].

web_blocks.takeaway: Even after a 38.5% drawdown from its high, Stallion trades at 39.6x to 46.2x trailing earnings while its net cash buffer is draining rapidly into delayed, cost-overrunning plants.

web_blocks.html: Do not treat Stallion's September 2026 cash balance as surplus cash on top of future plant earnings. In our 13 November dossier, ₹400 crore of March 2026 net cash (₹34.43 per share) looked like a firm cushion [1]. November 2026 filings broke that view. Cash and bank balances fell ₹141.97 crore in six months to ₹291.70 crore [36]. Other Current Assets jumped sevenfold to ₹160.88 crore, led by ₹129 crore of unmapped cost-plus-10% advances to Pansen Engineering [36][38]. On 19 November, management said roughly ₹50 crore of rights cash remained unspent [36]. It also flagged another ₹200 crore funding need across R-32 working capital, the ₹40 crore Bhilwara overrun, Mambattu, and HFO capex [36]. Cash spent to build plants cannot also count as excess cash.

Adjusting for the Q2 ESOP charge does not rescue the multiple either. A ₹9.51 crore two-quarter ESOP catch-up on 15,86,505 face-value options drove part of the Q2 profit drop, with ~₹4.7 crore per quarter continuing in H2 FY27 [36]. Adding back that entire charge treats real equity dilution as free. Even then, trailing operating profit rises from ₹53.1 crore to ₹62.6 crore, leaving EV to EBITDA at 27.3x. Strip out both ESOPs and ₹3.34 crore of treasury income, and core Q2 operating profit fell to ₹12.50 crore [36]. Core margin dropped to 9.19%—down 557 bps year on year and 896 bps sequentially [14][36]. Paying 40 times reported profit for a 9% margin business with negative cash flow leaves no safety margin.

web_blocks.title: Reverse DCF: what ₹171.59 still forces you to believe

web_blocks.html: A reverse DCF turns today's price into a required growth rate. We test the ten-year profit growth needed to justify Stallion's ₹1,708 crore ex-cash value and its ₹1,992 crore full market cap. We test a 12.5% base cost of equity, a 14.0% governance-adjusted hurdle, and 5.0% terminal growth [1][14][36].

web_blocks.takeaway: At ₹171.59 the market still demands 19.2% to 22.5% annual profit compounding for a full decade—even though cumulative operating cash flow is negative and both flagship plants just slipped out of FY27.

web_blocks.html: We used net profit as a proxy here because Stallion has not earned positive free cash flow since FY22. Free cash flow was −₹75 crore in FY24, −₹18 crore in FY25, and −₹10 crore in FY26 [1][24]. Operating cash flow then fell to −₹39.17 crore in H1 FY27 before capex [36]. That proxy flatters the business. Even so, ₹171.59 demands 19% to 22% annual profit growth for ten years. Sales must reach ₹2,540 to ₹3,320 crore—six to nearly eight times FY26 sales—without margin loss or dilution.

web_blocks.title: Re-underwritten FY28 scenarios: removing double-counted cash and pricing governance risk

web_blocks.html: Our prior 13 November valuation used a flat 30x FY28 multiple plus ₹34.43 per share of March cash, giving a ₹233.4 base value. November filings broke both pillars. Bhilwara R-32 slipped to May 2027 stabilization with a ₹40 crore overrun, and Mambattu slipped to early FY28 [36][37][38]. Both deliver zero FY27 revenue. September net cash of ₹284.7 crore will be fully spent on plants and ₹150 crore of R-32 working capital, leaving zero surplus FY28 cash and a ₹200 crore funding gap [36]. CARE Ratings' deviation flag, unmapped EPC advances, the GST search, and the 20.1-point promoter drop warrant a clear multiple discount to SRF's 32.7x [33][37][38][39][40].

web_blocks.caption: Re-underwritten FY28 equity scenarios on current 11.61 crore shares with zero surplus FY28 cash (compared to ₹171.59 live TradingView close) [14][32][36][37][38]
rows: Bear (plant lag, R-32 glut, governance drag)
web_blocks.takeaway: Once spent cash is no longer double-counted and exit multiples reflect governance and oversupply risk, FY28 Base falls from ₹233.4 to ₹143.2 (−16.5% vs ₹171.59; −20.7% vs ₹180.48), and drops further to ₹109.4 (25x) or ₹78.8 (18x) once debt interest and already-vesting ESOPs are charged.

web_blocks.html: Two baseline stress tests show how thin any floor really is. First, our headline bear case uses 22x depressed profit—about 1.0x September book value of ₹61.3 per share [14]. At a standard 15x trough chemical multiple on 11.61 crore shares, bear value drops to ₹42.0 per share (−75.5%). Second, the headline table assumes debt fills the ₹200 crore gap without equity issuance. If Stallion instead issues ₹200 crore of equity at ₹150 per share (+1.33 crore shares) plus 15.87 lakh ESOPs (+0.16 crore), share count jumps 12.9% to 13.10 crore [36]. That equity-funded dilution cuts Base from ₹143.2 to ₹126.9, Bear to ₹54.6 (or ₹37.2 at 15x), and Bull to ₹282.8.

A Red-Team Debt-Interest & ESOP-Dilution Stress Audit shows that even our debt-funded Base Case (₹143.2) is still generous. If debt fills the ₹200 crore gap at an assumed 10% pre-tax rate, annual post-tax interest costs ₹15.0 crore at a 25% tax rate (FY26 effective tax was 25.67%) [1][36]. That cuts Base PAT from ₹66.5 crore to ₹51.5 crore (7.36% net margin). Adding the already-granted 15.87 lakh one-year-vesting ESOPs (+0.16 crore) lifts minimum FY28 shares to 11.77 crore [36]. Base value then falls from ₹143.2 to ₹109.4 at 25x (−36.3%) and to ₹78.8 at an 18x governance/oversupply multiple (−54.1%). Replacing Bear's 22x multiple (₹61.6) with 15x yields ₹41.4 on 11.77 crore shares (−75.9%) or ₹37.2 on 13.10 crore shares (−78.3%). That cuts probability-weighted value from ₹132.9 to ₹97.4 (−43.3%) and drops the 12.5% hurdle re-entry price from ₹105.0 to ~₹76.9—reinforcing our hard REJECTED (TIER_0, 0%) posture.

Even before that debt-interest audit, our 9.5% base net margin is fair to management. Trailing net margin was 9.1% on ₹472.1 crore of sales, helped by ₹10 crore of treasury other income [14][24]. As cash drains into plants, other income will shrink while debt or financing costs rise. Bhilwara Phase 1 also omits upstream AHF production [36]. Management itself noted coming Indian R-32 capacity of ~80,000 MTPA is four times domestic demand of ~20,000 MTPA [36]. Against that supply wave, a 9.5% net margin is balanced, not harsh.

web_blocks.title: Peers: integrated rivals compound while Stallion compresses

web_blocks.html: Comparing Stallion with the three prospectus fluorochemical peers exposes a sharp margin and multiple gap on the 25 November live TradingView snapshot [7][32][33][34][35].

web_blocks.caption: Stallion versus prospectus fluorochemical peers: live TradingView valuation, profitability, growth, and Weinstein stage (retrieved 26 November 2026 UTC for the 25 November 2026 NSE close) [32][33][34][35]
web_blocks.takeaway: Stallion trades at 39.6x TradingView P/E (43.6x on Screener reported EPS) with 11.2% trailing operating margin, 8.4% ROE, and negative 9.9% EPS growth—more expensive than backward-integrated leader SRF at 32.7x P/E with 18.8% margin and +41.1% EPS growth.

web_blocks.html: Q2 FY27 results proved Stallion's margin drop was not an industry slump. In the exact quarter Stallion's core margin fell 557 bps to 9.19% (2.20% reported), integrated peers thrived on R-32 [36][42][43][44]. Navin Fluorine grew Q2 sales 57% to ₹1,191 crore at a 34.2% EBITDA margin [42]. It also commissioned 15,000 MTPA of R-32 at Surat and extended its ~$590 million HFO contract to 2032 [42]. Gujarat Fluorochemicals grew Q2 sales 45.5% to ₹1,760 crore at a 26.9% margin as fluorochemicals jumped 135% [43]. SRF earned ₹527.8 crore of Chemicals EBIT at a 25.4% margin while building 30,000 MTPA of captive AHF in Odisha [44].

That gap is structural. On 18 September 2026, DGTR recommended five more years of anti-dumping duty on Chinese R-32 imports [41]. SRF led the petition, backed by Gujarat Fluorochemicals and Navin Fluorine [41]. Integrated Indian rivals earn wide R-32 margins behind that tariff wall using captive inputs. Stallion imports 85% of sales in raw materials—92.97% from China—with no long-term contracts or captive AHF [6][36]. Continued duties squeeze Stallion's spreads while helping rivals. Paying 39.6x to 46.2x for Stallion over SRF at 32.7x makes no sense.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
paragraphs: Stallion raised ₹525 crore in fourteen months, spent most of it before Bhilwara sold one kilogram, and now wants ₹200 crore more. That cash balance is no longer a valuation floor; it is a dilution overhang. Once you stop double-counting spent cash, fair value drops below today's price.
Peer multiples settle the rest. Paying a higher P/E for an import-reliant blender with governance flags than for backward-integrated SRF breaks basic capital discipline.

book_paragraphs: Now we come to the price, and I want to be completely clear about why the valuation answer flipped sharply between 13 November and 25 November 2026. On the verified 23 November NSE market-facts ledger, Stallion closed at 180.48 rupees. Two trading days later, on the 25 November live TradingView close, it fell another 4.93% to 171.59 rupees. At 171.59 rupees, the stock is down 38.5% from its 52-week high of 279 rupees. Many retail investors look at a 38% drop and assume the risk has been wrung out of the price. The arithmetic says the opposite.

At 171.59 rupees across 11.61 crore shares, the Screener-basis market capitalisation is 1,992 crore rupees, while TradingView shows 2,104 crore on its vendor share basis. Against trailing reported earnings per share of 3.94 rupees, the stock trades at 43.6 times earnings. Screener reports 46.2 times on market value divided by trailing net profit of 43.1 crore, and TradingView displays 39.6 times. Whichever vendor column you choose, you are paying roughly forty to forty-six times trailing profit for a company whose latest quarterly operating profit fell to 2.99 crore and whose six-month operating cash flow relapsed to negative 39.17 crore.

In our previous edition, the balance sheet softened that harsh multiple. On the audited March 2026 accounts, Stallion held 400 crore of net cash, or 34.43 rupees per share, after its February 2026 rights issue. It was tempting to subtract that cash from the share price and treat it as a permanent safety cushion sitting alongside future plant profits. November 2026 filings destroyed that comfort. Between March and September 2026, cash and bank balances dropped by 142 crore to 291.7 crore, pulling September net cash down to 284.7 crore, or 24.52 rupees per share.

Even that September figure is already stale on the downside. On the 19 November earnings call, management confirmed that only roughly 50 crore of rights-issue proceeds remained unspent, while Infomerics revealed that 36 crore—nearly ten percent of the gross rights issue—went straight to issue expenses and 129 crore sat in unmapped capital advances to civil contractor Pansen Engineering. Worse, management outlined a fresh 200 crore incremental external funding requirement—alongside remaining rights cash, accruals, the unused 120 crore overdraft, and deferred late-2027 HFO timing—to bridge 400 to 405 crore of combined uses across 150 crore of R-32 working capital, a 40 crore cost overrun at Bhilwara, a 10 to 15 crore shortfall at Mambattu, and 200 crore of future HFO plant spending. When every rupee of cash in the bank is already spoken for and you still need 200 crore more, you do not have surplus cash to add on top of your FY28 earnings valuation. Counting that cash twice is how investors talk themselves into overpaying.

Let us test the price fairly on the ESOP noise too. In the September quarter, Stallion booked a 9.51 crore non-cash ESOP charge covering two quarters on 15.87 lakh face-value options, with roughly 4.7 crore per quarter still to come in the second half of FY27. Some investors will wave that away because no cash left the bank account. I do not wave away face-value stock options, because giving insiders equity at ten rupees a share transfers real ownership away from outside shareholders. Yet even if you grant management's argument and add back the entire 9.51 crore charge, trailing operating profit rises only to 62.6 crore. Against an ex-cash enterprise value of 1,708 crore, that is still 27.3 times operating profit. Meanwhile, stripping out both ESOPs and 3.34 crore of treasury other income shows that core operating profit in the September quarter dropped to 12.50 crore, a 9.19% margin—down more than five and a half percentage points from a year earlier. The core spread compressed even before accounting adjustments.

A reverse discounted cash flow model strips away narrative optimism and tells you the exact growth rate embedded in 171.59 rupees. Because Stallion's free cash flow has been negative in FY24, FY25, FY26, and the first half of FY27, I had to use accounting net profit as a generous proxy for cash earnings. At a 12.5% cost of equity and 5% terminal growth after year ten, justifying the 1,708 crore ex-cash enterprise value on FY26 profit of 43.8 crore requires profit to compound at 19.2% every year for a decade—reaching 254 crore of profit on roughly 2,540 crore of revenue at a ten percent net margin. If you recognize that there is no surplus cash and make the operating business justify the full 1,992 crore market capitalisation, the required ten-year profit growth jumps to 21.4% a year, demanding over 3,040 crore in year-ten sales. Add a modest 150 basis-point governance risk premium to lift the hurdle rate to 14%, and the price demands 22.5% annual profit compounding for ten straight years. Even on an ex-ESOP profit base of 52 crore, the market demands 16.8% compounding for a decade.

That brings us to our re-underwritten FY28 scenarios, where the gap between our prior report and today's reality becomes unmistakable. Because both Bhilwara R-32 and Mambattu slipped again and will deliver zero revenue in FY27, FY28 is the first year either plant can contribute meaningfully. In the base case, I assume Bhilwara begins phased production in April 2027, stabilizes in May, and helps lift FY28 revenue to 700 crore—a 27.5% two-year annual growth rate from FY26, which is still ambitious given repeated execution misses. With non-AHF-integrated R-32 economics, ongoing ESOP expenses, shrinking treasury interest income, and new financing costs, I model a 9.5% net margin, yielding 66.5 crore of FY28 net profit. Applying a 25 times multiple—a disciplined discount to SRF's 32.7 times multiple given Stallion's monitoring-agency qualifications, GST search, and cash-flow relapse—with zero surplus cash left on the balance sheet yields 143.2 rupees per share. That is 16.5% below the 25 November live price and 20.7% below the 23 November ledger close.

In the bear case, Bhilwara lags further or runs straight into an Indian R-32 supply glut—remember that management itself noted coming Indian capacity of 80,000 tonnes against just 20,000 tonnes of domestic demand—while Chinese anti-dumping duties keep import spreads tight and governance worries persist. Revenue stalls at 500 crore and net margins slip back to 6.5%, earning 32.5 crore of net profit. At 22 times depressed earnings—roughly one times September 2026 book value of 61.3 rupees per share—bear value is 61.6 rupees, down 64% from 171.59 rupees. And if the market refuses to hold book value and values a troubled chemical trader at a cyclical 15 times trough multiple, bear value falls to 42 rupees, a 75% wipeout.

To be fair to the other side, I still model an explicit bull case. If Bhilwara stabilizes cleanly in May 2027, Mambattu and Khalapur helium ramp smoothly, R-32 prices hold firm ahead of the 2028 Kigali freeze, and governance controls are overhauled, revenue could reach 950 crore at a 13% net margin for 123.5 crore of profit. At 30 times earnings, the bull case reaches 319.1 rupees per share, up 86% from today's price. That upside is real in arithmetic, which is why the stock still attracts speculative buyers. The problem is that you have to absorb extreme dilution, execution, and governance risk just to reach a modest probability-weighted outcome, as chapter 9 will quantify.

There is one more number every shareholder must write in the margin: equity dilution and debt financing cost. The headline scenarios divide FY28 equity value by today's 11.61 crore shares, assuming management covers its 200 crore funding gap with debt. If management instead issues 200 crore of fresh equity at 150 rupees a share through a QIP or preferential allotment alongside the 15.87 lakh ESOP options already granted, diluted share count reaches 13.10 crore—a 12.9% expansion that drops Base from 143.2 to 126.9 rupees, Bear to 54.6 (or 37.2 at 15 times), and Bull to 282.8 rupees. Even under the debt-funded path, a Red-Team stress audit shows the headline Base is still generous: charging an assumed 10% pre-tax rate on 200 crore of debt (15.0 crore post-tax at 25% tax) cuts Base PAT from 66.5 to 51.5 crore (a 7.36% net margin), and adding the 15.87 lakh already-vesting ESOPs (+0.16 crore to 11.77 crore shares) cuts Base to 109.4 rupees at 25 times (−36.3%) and 78.8 rupees at an 18 times governance multiple (−54.1%). Pairing that with a 15 times trough Bear multiple (41.4 rupees on 11.77 crore shares) pulls probability-weighted value down from 132.9 to 97.4 rupees (−43.3%) and drops the 12.5% hurdle re-entry price from 105.0 to roughly 76.9 rupees.

Finally, look across the fence at the three peers named in Stallion's own prospectus, because peer comparison settles the debate with zero ambiguity. On the 25 November live TradingView snapshot, Navin Fluorine trades at 56.1 times earnings with a 30.3% operating margin, 45.7% trailing revenue growth, and 22.6% return on equity; in the September quarter alone, it posted a 34.2% EBITDA margin, commissioned 15,000 tonnes of R-32 capacity, and extended its multi-year HFO contract through 2032. Gujarat Fluorochemicals trades at 76.6 times trailing earnings, grew Q2 revenue 45.5% with a 26.9% EBITDA margin, and surged 135% in fluorochemicals on R-32. And SRF—an integrated national leader earning an 18.8% trailing operating margin, 25.4% Chemicals EBIT margin in Q2, 16% return on equity, and 41% trailing EPS growth—trades at just 32.7 times earnings.

Pause on that contrast. Stallion trades at 39.6 times on TradingView and 43.6 to 46.2 times on Screener, with an 11.2% trailing operating margin, 8.4% return on equity, negative 9.9% EPS growth, and zero upstream AHF integration. Meanwhile, SRF, Gujarat Fluorochemicals, and Navin Fluorine successfully petitioned India's trade authority in September 2026 for a five-year continuation of anti-dumping duties on Chinese R-32—a tariff wall that widens their integrated profits while squeezing Stallion's China-imported blending spreads until Bhilwara actually works. Paying a premium multiple to SRF for a non-integrated smaller player facing cost overruns, monitoring-agency qualifications, and a third capital raise is a bad trade in any market cycle. Chapter 8 now checks whether the tape agrees with that arithmetic.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Never add committed construction cash on top of future factory earnings. Once you stop double-counting Stallion's draining bank balance and compare its 40-plus multiple against SRF at 32.7 times, the valuation stops looking like a bargain on a dip and reveals itself as an expensive bet on unproven execution.
